Posted November 27, 2007 

Analysis by Richard Cowan  

 

I have written about potent pot and the prohibitionist party line many times, since Marijuana Prohibition And Potency, Price, And Safety -- "Is Marijuana Stronger Now Than It Was Back In the '60s, When Everyone Thought It Was Harmless?" on August 11, 1998.  

See 

Time Magazine Reports BC Bud 20% Less Potent Than Four Years Ago??  Incompetent Prohibitionist Propaganda and Even Worse Journalism. As Some Reporters Die to Find the Truth Others Live to Lie.
and 

Potent Pot Myth Undermined By Report From The Ultimate Authority. Cited By Swedish Prohibitionist Who Dont Seem To Understand. As Usual.  

But lets start at the beginning.  

 

In 1986, I wrote an article for National Review magazine, How the Narks Create Crack, in which I argued, The iron law of drug prohibition is that the more intense the law enforcement, the more potent the drugs will become. The latest stage of this cycle has brought us the crack epidemic. There are two inescapable reasons for this.  

 

First, from the supply perspective, it is good business to minimize the bulk of contraband. Obviously, the bulkiest illegal drug, marijuana, will lose out in the supply channels to cocaine and heroin.  

 

Marijuana remains the principal target of law-enforcement efforts, despite the current crack-generated headlines. One result is that the weed, which can be grown anywhere, is being cultivated in more potent strains to justify a higher price per pound. (emphasis added) 

 

Now skip forward to 1997, when my good friends, Dr. John Morgan and the late Prof. Lynn Zimmer, were writing their book Marijuana Myths; Marijuana Facts.  

 

I remember Dr. Morgan joking and saying that when they began the chapter on potency he was sure that they would find that it had increased because of what I had written in National Review. But, according to the governments own data, the average THC levels had been in the 3% to 4% range for years. 

 

However, what they did find was that the prohibitionist had been making the same claims since the 1970s, while at the same time misusing data from very limited samples from that period to claim that marijuana had only traces of THC back in the sixties when we all thought that it was harmless as we sometimes still hear them say. (There is no data from the 1960s.) 

 

They also found that some samples that were privately tested in the 1970s had THC levels as high as 14%. So, as all of us of a certain age already knew, there is nothing new about good weed.  

 

Ironically, the data for 1997 was not yet available, and that was the first year in which the potency of all grades of marijuana (including sinsemilla) appeared to begin moving above the 4% where it had been for years, if we can believe the governments graph, which I first used in commenting on the governments claim that the marijuana was going to be flooded this year.  

 

Having read so many prohibitionist lies, I should have realized that the narks had not suddenly started to tell the truth. The number that they use is an average of the marijuana and the sinsemilla  which would be alright, if we knew how representative of the whole market their samples are.  

 

They acknowledge that most of the market is still Mexican marijuana, but there is simply no way that we can know how much of the total supply is domestic or imported indoor sinsemilla (the strongest), domestic outdoor, destroyed in vast quantities, esp. in California, (good seeds, but not usually sinsemilla) and Mexican of all grades, which is seized in vast quantities at the border. (Only weed that is seized at or after harvest can be accurately tested.)   

 

The validity and meaning of the testing data depends on how much of each is seized, how the police choose samples to be sent for testing, which is probably biased toward the stronger smelling samples, and how representative of the total market these samples are.  

 

Without knowing the size of each of these, especially the total market size, we can never know the real average potency.   

 

Brian Bennett gives the full data through 2004, which shows the increase in both sinsemilla and Mexican potency really beginning in 1997.  

 

This increase in sinsemilla potency and prevalence was the result of efforts by Dutch and American breeders (some of whom were in Holland) and seed merchants in Holland and Canada.  

 

As their products  and the knowledge about how to grow indoors  spread, sinsemillas share of the market started to soar.  

 

Nederwiet replaced smuggled hash in the Dutch coffee shops. At the same time the Dutch continued improving their growing methods and genetics. According to Trimbos.nl, the Netherlands Institute of Mental Health and Addiction, THC content in Dutch nederwiet averaged 11.3 per cent in 2000, compared to 8.6 per cent in 1996. Then it increased until, the average THC content of Dutch-grown weed dropped from a level of 20% in 2004 to 18% in 2005 and 2006.  

 

Notice that the increase in THC levels happened in both the US and Holland at about the same time. 

 

This report would seem to indicate that it is difficult to sustain production of plants with THC levels above 18% or so. Also, Dutch coffee shops report that many customers do not want the strongest weed.  

 

Nonetheless, it should be understood that  although buying and selling small amounts of cannabis is tolerated  the supply side is still illegal, and a lot of Nederwiet is smuggled into  or bought by citizens of  other countries. In other words, it is still contraband.   

 

As I have often said, the prohibitionist party line is international. The Brit prohibitionists have gone even more bonkers over what they call skunk.  

 

Here is how Ben Goldacre, the Guardians Bad Science editor put it on March 24th : 

Laboratory of the Government Chemistdata on mean potency goes from 1975 to 1989. Resin pootles around between 6% and 10% THC, herbal between 4% and 6%, with no clear trend. The Forensic Science Service data takes over to produce more modern figures, showing not much change in resin, and domestically produced indoor herbal cannabis doubling in strength to between 12% and 14%. 

 

The rising trend of cannabis potency is gradual, and driven largely by the increased availability of intensively UK grown indoor herbal cannabis. You could argue that intensive indoor cultivation of a plant that is easy to cultivate outdoors is the cannabis industry's reaction to illegality. It is dangerous to import in large amounts, dangerous to be caught growing a field of it. So perhaps it makes more sense to grow it intensively indoors, producing a more concentrated product. There is little incentive to produce a perversely strong skunk product for the mass market, since most people tend not to pay any more for unusually strong skunk. 

 

There is exceptionally strong cannabis to be found in some parts of the UK market today: but there always has been. The UN Drug Control Programme has detailed vintage data for the UK online. In 1975 the LGC analysed 50 seized samples of herbal cannabis: 10 were from Thailand, with an average potency of 7.8%, the highest 17%. In 1975 they analysed 11 samples of seized resin, six from Morocco, average strength 9%, with a range from 4% to 16%. 

 

To get their scare figure, the Independent compared the worst cannabis from the past with the best cannabis of today. But you could have cooked the books the same way 30 years ago: in 1975 the weakest herbal cannabis analysed was 0.2%; in 1978 the strongest was 12%. Oh my god: in just three years herbal cannabis has become 60 times stronger. This scare isn't new. In the US, in the mid 1980s, during Reagan's "war on drugs", it was claimed that cannabis was 14 times stronger than in 1970. 

 

Meanwhile back in Bushlandia, we can certainly assume that the average potency is now well above 5%, especially away from the Mexican border. This means that the proposed Massachusetts decrim initiative, which applies only to cannabis with a maximum of 2.5%, less than half of the national average, is meaningless, at best.  

See 

Dr. Grinspoon Opposes Massachusetts Decrim Initiative As Fatally Flawed. Internal Possession Of Marijuana Metabolites?!! 

The point of all this data is simply that what I called the iron law of drug prohibition applies everywhere.  

 

In the UK, cannabis has increased in average potency, as it has in Holland and the US. However, in the US and the UK, hard drug use is much higher than in Holland, where cannabis is very easy to get. The markets for hard and soft drugs have been separated. The gateway of the black market has been closed. 

 

The bottom line is simply that marijuana prohibition and the drug war in general should not been seen as merely a failure, but as a massive counterproductive fraud that is making the all of our problems much worse  at a vast expense in lives and treasures lost.
